summary:
Côte d'Ivoire does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices states that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground. The sources assembled here do not cover entry, visa or identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers.

Non-state violence against LGBTQ people is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report records three deaths within the community during that year. Police responses to violence committed by non-state actors were described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often blaming the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Peer research published in Critical African Studies in 2015 found that Ivoirian travestis, women identified at birth who live as women, endure harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender presentation attracts less attention.

The UNDP's December 2024 review of African Commission Resolution 275 includes a Côte d'Ivoire overview assessing the protective legal environment, the investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space, and the inclusion of LGBT+ people. A New York Times article dated October 2024 also addresses the situation of LGBTQ people in the country.
tangentialFactors:
The 2015 Critical African Studies study situates the exclusion of travestis within the aftermath of the 2010-11 post-election crisis, which the US State Department's 2011 human rights report documents as producing some 3,000 deaths, widespread sexual violence and mass displacement. That crisis context shapes how authorities and communities respond to gender-nonconforming people today.

Ivoirian rights groups have historically distanced themselves from travestis, leaving them underserved by the very organisations that might otherwise assist a person in trouble. This pattern of exclusion within advocacy structures is a distinct risk factor from state hostility.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing documentation on the placement of transgender detainees is absent from the sources reviewed. Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire; where trans detainees are placed, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any listed publication. On the Human Rights Watch country page for Côte d'Ivoire, 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link.

The 2015 Critical African Studies study documents both the violence and social exclusion experienced by travestis in Côte d'Ivoire and their resilience, and is archived in PubMed Central.
outOfScopeNotes:
Entry, visa and identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers are not covered by any source in this inventory. Whether a visitor's passport gender marker affects processing at Ivorian border control remains unresolved and not sourced.

The inventory does not establish whether Côte d'Ivoire recognises a legal gender marker change, whether any anti-discrimination statute explicitly covers gender identity, or whether hate-crime enhancements apply to bias-motivated violence against trans people. These questions are not addressed in the listed materials.

The 2011 US State Department report contains limited LGBT-specific content and is used here only for the post-electoral crisis context; it does not speak to the current legal position of trans visitors.
